title: Michaelmas and Harvest
also: Feast of St Michael and All Angels
when_text: 29 September; Old Michaelmas Day 10-11 October; harvest festivals on a Sunday in September or October
intro: Michaelmas, the feast of St Michael and All Angels on 29 September, closed the farming year: the harvest was in, rents and accounts were settled and servants hired for the year ahead. It brought goose dinners, hiring fairs and the warning not to pick blackberries after the devil had spoiled them, and St Michael's churches stand on hilltops and sea rocks across the isles. The church harvest festival is younger than most people think: it began in a Cornish parish in 1843.

facts.title: A quarter day for rents and reckonings
facts.text: Michaelmas, 29 September, was one of the four English quarter days, kept in Wales and the Channel Islands too, when rents fell due, servants were hired and accounts had to be settled. In Ireland it was a 'gale day' when rent was owed.

sources.title: Quarter days (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The English quarter days (also observed in Wales and the Channel Islands) are Lady Day (25 March, the Feast of the Annunciation); Midsummer Day (24 June, the Feast of the Nativity of St John the Baptist); Michaelmas Day (29 September

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The day was also considered a "gale day" in Ireland when rent would be due

facts.title: The end of the farming year
facts.text: On the medieval manor Michaelmas closed one farming year and opened the next: the harvest was in, the reeve drew up the year's accounts, and on many manors a new reeve was chosen from among the peasants.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: At that time harvest was over, and the bailiff or reeve of the manor would be making out the accounts for the year.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: On manors, it was the day when a reeve was elected from the peasants.

facts.title: The Michaelmas goose
facts.text: A stubble goose, fattened on the gleanings of the harvest fields, was the dish of the day, and eating one was said to keep you in money all year. Tenants sometimes paid geese to their landlords; the custom goes back at least to the 15th century. The story that Elizabeth I began it on hearing of the Armada's defeat does not fit the dates.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There was a saying that "if you eat goose on Michaelmas Day you will never lack money all year".

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The custom dates to at least the 15th century, and was easily continued as geese are in their prime at Michaelmas time.

facts.title: The devil and the blackberries
facts.text: Folklore across the isles says blackberries should not be picked after Michaelmas, or after Old Michaelmas Day (10 or 11 October): when St Michael threw the devil out of heaven he landed in a bramble bush and spoiled the fruit. In Yorkshire he spat on them; in Cornwall the story is ruder.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is said that when St. Michael expelled the devil, Lucifer, from heaven, he fell from the skies and landed in a prickly blackberry bush.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: According to Morrell (1977), this old legend is well known in all parts of Great Britain, even as far north as the Orkney Islands.

facts.title: Hiring fairs and the mop
facts.text: Hiring fairs, also called statute or mop fairs, go back to Edward III's labour laws after the Black Death. Workers stood with a token of their trade, a tuft of wool for a shepherd, and once hired spent their earnest money at the fair's stalls. After the calendar change of 1752 the mops moved to Old Michaelmas Day; Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwick, Tewkesbury and other Midlands towns still hold them as funfairs.

sources.title: Mop fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: They date from the time of Edward III, and his attempt to regulate the labour market by the Statute of Labourers in 1351

sources.title: Mop fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This date is known as "Old Michaelmas Day" and since 1752 was the date of the mop fairs.

facts.title: Nottingham's Goose Fair
facts.text: Nottingham's fair had a royal charter from Edward I in 1284 and is first called 'Goose Fair' in the borough records of 1541. Up to 20,000 geese, their feet coated in tar and sand for the road, were driven from the fens to be sold in the Old Market Square for the Michaelmas table. The fair moved to early October in 1752 and is now a funfair.

sources.title: Goose Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The first reference to the name "Goose Fair" can be found in the Nottingham Borough Records of 1541

sources.title: Goose Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The geese were sold in Nottingham to provide the traditional Michaelmas dish of roast goose

facts.title: Harvest festival began in a Cornish parish
facts.text: The church harvest festival as it is kept today was begun in 1843 by the Revd Robert Stephen Hawker, vicar of Morwenstow in Cornwall, who invited his parishioners to a thanksgiving service and gave communion with bread from the first corn cut. Victorian hymns such as 'We plough the fields' spread the idea.

where.name: Church of St Morwenna and St John the Baptist, Morwenstow

sources.title: Harvest festival (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The modern British tradition of celebrating the Harvest Festival in churches began in 1843, when the Reverend Robert Hawker invited parishioners to a special thanksgiving service at his church at Morwenstow in Cornwall.

sources.title: Robert Stephen Hawker (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This service took place on 1 October and bread made from the first cut of corn was taken at communion.

facts.title: Harvest home and the last sheaf
facts.text: Before the church festival, the end of harvest was a farm affair: a harvest supper, or mell-supper, for everyone who had helped, after the last stand of corn was cut. Nobody wanted to cut it, so in some counties the reapers threw their sickles at it or took turns blindfolded with a scythe.

sources.title: Harvest festival (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was sometimes known as a "Mell-supper", after the last patch of corn or wheat standing in the fields which were known as the "Mell" or "Neck".

sources.title: Harvest festival (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: There seems to have been a feeling that it was bad luck to be the person to cut the last stand of corn.

facts.title: Crying the Neck in Cornwall and Devon
facts.text: In Devon and Cornwall the last handful of corn, the 'neck', was held up while the reapers shouted 'A neck! A neck!'. The Old Cornwall Society revived the custom after the Second World War and still organises it.

sources.title: Crying the Neck (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In Cornwall there was an organised revival of the practice on five farms in the 20 years after the Second World War by the Old Cornwall Society

sources.title: Crying the Neck (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: "A neck! A neck! A neck!"

facts.title: Corn dollies, the Kirn Baby and the harvest mare
facts.text: The last sheaf was often plaited into a figure kept for luck until the next sowing. Its names change across the isles: the Kirn Baby in the Lothians, the Kern Baby in Northumberland, the Cailleach (the old woman) in Gaelic Scotland, and the caseg fedi or harvest mare in Wales.

sources.title: Corn dolly (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Kirn Baby (Lothians) Kern Baby (Northumberland)

sources.title: Corn dolly (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Caseg Fedi or harvest mare in Wales

facts.title: St Michael's bannock
facts.text: In the Hebrides a special bread, the struan or St Michael's bannock, was baked on Michaelmas Eve from barley, oats and rye, made without any metal tool. Some were blessed and given to the poor in memory of the dead.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The bread was made from equal parts of barley, oats, and rye without using any metal implements.

facts.title: Michaelmas in Ireland
facts.text: In Ireland people went on pilgrimage to holy wells of St Michael, the goose was eaten or given to the poor, and in Tramore, County Waterford, an effigy of the saint called the Micilín was carried to the shore to mark the end of the fishing season.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In Tramore, County Waterford, a procession with an effigy of St Michael, called the Micilín, was brought through the town to the shore to mark the end of the fishing season.

facts.title: Michaelmas term and a new Lord Mayor
facts.text: Michaelmas still names the autumn term at Oxford, Cambridge, Durham and Dublin, and the first of the legal terms. In the City of London the liverymen meet at Guildhall on Michaelmas Day to elect the next Lord Mayor, by a show of hands.

sources.title: Michaelmas (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: These include the universities of Cambridge, London, Durham, Lancaster, Oxford, Swansea, and Dublin.

sources.title: Lord Mayor of London (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It meets at Guildhall on Michaelmas Day (29 September) or on the closest weekday. Voting is by show of hands.

facts.title: Michael of the high places
facts.text: St Michael, the angel who fought the dragon, is the patron of many hills and high rocks, and his churches crown Glastonbury Tor, St Michael's Mount, Brent Tor and Skellig Michael. Glastonbury's first church on the Tor was thrown down by the earthquake of 11 September 1275.

sources.title: Glastonbury Tor (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: because of the long-standing dedication to St. Michael the Archangel (the patron of many sacred mountains and hills)

sources.title: Glastonbury Tor (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St Michael's Church was destroyed by an earthquake on 11 September 1275.

places.name: Glastonbury Tor and St Michael's Tower
places.why: The roofless tower of St Michael's church tops the Tor. The second church, built in the 14th century after the earthquake of 1275, stood until the Dissolution of 1539.

sources.title: Glastonbury Tor (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: A second church, also dedicated to St Michael, was built of local sandstone in the 14th century by the Abbot Adam of Sodbury

places.name: St Michael's Mount
places.why: A tidal island crowned by a castle and the 15th-century chapel of St Michael, once a priory of Mont-Saint-Michel in Normandy and a place of pilgrimage.

sources.title: St Michael's Mount (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The chapel of St Michael, a 15th-century building, has an embattled tower

sources.title: St Michael's Mount (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It was a priory of that Mont-Saint-Michel until the dissolution of the alien houses

places.name: Skellig Michael
places.why: The monastery on this Atlantic rock off Kerry was dedicated to St Michael by about 1044, perhaps as early as 950, when St Michael's Church was added; it stands about 180 m above the sea.

sources.title: Skellig Michael (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The site had been dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel by at least 1044

sources.title: Skellig Michael (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: St. Michael's Church dates to the 10th or early 11th century.

places.name: St Michael de Rupe, Brent Tor
places.why: The little church of 'St Michael of the Rock' sits on a volcanic tor on the edge of Dartmoor. Legend says the devil kept moving the building stones to the hilltop to stop it being built.

sources.title: Brent Tor (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Church of St Michel de Rupe ("Saint Michael of the Rock") atop the Tor dates to the 12th century

sources.title: Brent Tor (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: the devil who didn't want to see its construction would move the construction to the top of the hill each night

places.name: Ysgyryd Fawr (Skirrid Fawr)
places.why: The 'Holy Mountain' near Abergavenny has the ruins of a medieval chapel of St Michael on its summit. Pilgrims climbed it on Michaelmas Eve, and in 1676 the Pope offered an indulgence to those who went up at Michaelmas.

sources.title: Skirrid Fawr (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Christian pilgrimages were traditionally made, especially on Michaelmas Eve, to the summit.

sources.title: Skirrid Fawr (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: In 1676, Pope Clement X promised a plenary indulgence to those who went up the mountain upon Michaelmas.

places.name: Church of St Morwenna and St John the Baptist, Morwenstow
places.why: Robert Hawker's church, where he held the first modern harvest festival in 1843.

sources.title: Robert Stephen Hawker (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The Harvest Festival that we know today was introduced in the parish of Morwenstow in 1843 by Hawker.

places.name: Hawker's Hut, Morwenstow
places.why: The driftwood hut on the cliffs where Hawker wrote his poems; it is the National Trust's smallest property.

sources.title: Robert Stephen Hawker (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: This driftwood hut is now the smallest property in the National Trust portfolio.

places.name: Old Market Square, Nottingham
places.why: For hundreds of years Goose Fair was held here, with thousands of geese driven in along Goose Gate.

sources.title: Goose Fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: It is recorded that up to 20,000 geese were driven up through Hockley and along "Goose Gate" into Nottingham's Old Market Square

places.name: Guildhall, London
places.why: Common Hall meets here on Michaelmas Day to elect the Lord Mayor of London.

sources.title: Lord Mayor of London (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The lord/lady mayor is elected at Common Hall each year on Michaelmas

places.name: Church of the Holy Trinity, Stratford-upon-Avon
places.why: Stratford-upon-Avon is one of the old mop towns that still hold a mop fair each year around Michaelmas; Holy Trinity, the town's medieval parish church, is where Shakespeare is buried.

sources.title: Mop fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: The following towns have a history of holding mops and still hold one each year on or around Michaelmas Day.

sources.title: Mop fair (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: Stratford upon Avon Tewkesbury Warwick

sources.title: Church of the Holy Trinity, Stratford-upon-Avon (Wikipedia)
sources.author: Wikipedia contributors
sources.quote: due to its fame as the place of baptism and burial of William Shakespeare
